summary: Wario planned a treasure expedition in a locked room, hired a stranger named Jory Dobbs off a noticeboard for a wage of nothing, forged two passports, and specifically excluded Waluigi — then spotted him on a balcony with binoculars at four in the morning, abducted him in a produce sack, and flew a taped-together charter into a storm hunting treasure in Mount Ebott. The aircraft crashed into a cave, the pilot was knocked out, Dobbs took a head wound, and the party climbed anyway — past a bone-throwing teleporter, an earthquake that pushed skeletons up in rows, and a razor-and-flame trap bridge — to a summit plank reading MOUNT EBOT. One T. They had climbed the wrong mountain, and the map's own cartouche said whose fault it was.
imageCaption: Mount Ebot from the valley track, photographed on a later survey. One T. 1,340 feet of wet slate that cost an aircraft, a bridge crossing and eight years of filing delay. The board had been levered off the signpost and left face-down in the mud; the archive notes that removing a sign takes more effort than reading one.
description:
*"Your cut? Experience. An adventure. A story for the grandkids. Do you know what people pay for an adventure?"*
— **[Wario](#/article/wario)**, setting the expedition's wage structure

*"There is a mountain. There is treasure in the mountain. There is a man who told me about the mountain and I only had to hit him once."*
— **[Wario](#/article/wario)**, four o'clock in the morning, to a courtyard

*"So we climbed the wrong mountain."*
— **[Jory Dobbs](#/article/jory_dobbs)**, summit of Mount Ebot, bleeding

*"WAH! Every injury on this expedition, every bone, every razor, every burned name on every plank, descends from one absent letter in a printing house that no longer exists. Waluigi did not lose a day to a mountain. Waluigi lost a day to a compositor with cold hands."*
— **[Waluigi](#/article/waluigi)**, Auditor-General, Walupedia Editorial Board

---

Filed as a session record of 17 Aethel, 1032 BF, and released to the archive only now. The notebook went into a crate with the misprinted chart and the correction demand, and the crate went into storage behind eight years of more urgent disasters. Waluigi has changed nothing in it. The wound was dressed in 1032, the plank was read in 1032, and the correction the Old World Mapping Company promised on application has still not arrived. The expedition was planned the previous afternoon in a gold room Waluigi was deliberately excluded from — a room containing treasure maps weighted down with garlic bread, two forged passports, a journal describing an artifact called the Heartstone, and a young man being told that his share of the proceeds would be nothing. The first four sections of this filing reconstruct that afternoon from the hire's account and are marked as reconstruction. Everything after it is first-hand.

Waluigi was carried out of his own building in an agricultural sack at four in the morning and returned by air at twenty to ten that night, and in the eighteen hours between those two facts the expedition argued about satellite phones, discovered that Wario had packed thermal gear cut for a man he claimed not to be bringing, crashed an aircraft into a cave, hauled nine loads up a scree slope on a rope chain, was attacked by a silent four-foot figure that threw sharpened human bones and left by folding the air, watched a hillside open in parallel seams and hand back its dead, crossed a maintained trap bridge with sixty razors and six oil jets, recorded four missing humans from a burned plank with one name rubbed nearly out, and reached a summit cairn to discover from the expedition's own map that the mountain was **Mount Ebot** — one T — a different mountain entirely from Mount Ebott, printed by **The Old World Mapping Company, Survey Series IV, corrections on application.**

Waluigi speaks perhaps two hundred words aloud across the whole day. What follows includes the rest.

sections.name: I. The Villa, and the Chair That Fell Over
sections.overview:
Waluigi was not in this room. Waluigi wants that stated at the top, in the archive's own voice, because this section and the three that follow it are reconstruction, and the archive does not pretend otherwise. What follows was assembled afterward from the hire's account, given twice on two different days and consistent both times; from the state of the room, which Waluigi later saw; and from the fact that Wario is the single most predictable man alive and has never once surprised anybody who was paying attention.

The room was the long gold one on the ground floor of the villa. Treasure maps had been unrolled across the table and weighted at the corners with a candlestick, a stapler, and two ends of a torn loaf. There was garlic bread on the maps. There is always garlic bread on the maps.

**"Finally,"** Wario said, and brought both hands down flat on the table hard enough to make the paper jump. **"Took you long enough to show up. Mount Ebott. We're going back."**

The chair went over behind him when he stood — a solid backwards crash on marble that he did not turn around for, did not glance at, and did not right at any point in the following two hours. It was still lying there when the room was next opened.

**"I've been through the old explorer notes all week,"** he said, pacing the length of the table, stabbing a finger down at different parts of the map without appearing to look at where it landed. **"There's a vault in those peaks. We got close last time. Missed it by inches. Blizzard."**

The hire — twenty-two years old, in a woollen hat, standing where he had been told to stand — asked how close inches was.

**"Inches,"** Wario said.

Then he spun, and the spin took out a stack of gold-plated plates that went across the floor in a long bright clatter, and he did not look at those either.

**"Summer solstice. All those avalanche zones are melt by then. And I have got—"** and here his voice dropped into the register he believes is a whisper, leaning in until the boy could smell the garlic **"—*satellite images*. There's a structure under the ice. Something big."**

He crossed to a cabinet, unlocked it, and came back with a journal bound in cracked hide, holding it flat on two palms like a waiter.

**"Out of my private museum. Talks about an artifact. The Heartstone."** He let the name sit. **"Unlimited wealth. To whoever holds it. That is worth more than every share certificate in this building."**

*WAH! Observe the sequence. A vault becomes a structure becomes an artifact becomes unlimited wealth, and at no point in the escalation does a single verifiable object enter the room. Wario has photographs he will not produce and a journal he will not let go of. Waluigi has audited men who lied better than this while holding worse.*

The boy looked around the enormous gold room and asked whether anyone else was in it.

Wario stopped. He scanned the corners properly for the first time — the grandfather clock ticking against the far wall, the chandelier with its slow drip, the velvet curtain by the windows, which he walked over and pulled back to find nothing behind it but dust and more dust.

**"Nope. Just us. Guards are all outside today. Didn't want nosy ears."**

**"So no Waluigi,"** the boy said.

The face Wario made is recorded in the hire's account as *like he bit a bad egg*. **"That lanky weirdo? I told him to stay home. That guy could not keep a secret if you stapled it to his forehead."** The vase went next — a real one, off a plinth, into pieces across the marble. He did not look at that either. **"Last big thing we planned together he blabbed it at karaoke night and we nearly got picked up by Bowser's goons."**
sections.waluigi_note: Two of the three claims in that last sentence are false and the third is worse. Waluigi did not blab at karaoke; Wario sang the plan, in full, in a key of his own devising, to a room of forty people. The goons were already there. And Waluigi was not "told to stay home" in any sense that involved being told — he learned he was excluded eleven hours later, in a sack, at altitude. Wario does not lie so much as he pre-writes the version he intends to remember. WAH.

sections.name: II. Two Wallets, and the Word Nobody Wanted Said
sections.overview:
The briefing ended the way all Wario briefings end, which is with logistics presented as generosity.

He went back to the cabinet and came out with two wallets, and laid them on the map side by side with the air of a man dealing a winning hand.

**"Identification,"** he said. **"For the border, for the airfield, for anyone who asks. Yours and mine. Untraceable."**

They were passports of a sort — hard covers, plausible stamps, a lamination bubble in one corner of each. The first said **GREGORIO MORETTI**. The second said **HANS KÜBLER**. The photographs inside bore no resemblance to either man standing at the table, a fact the hire raised immediately and was answered as follows:

**"Nobody looks at the picture. They look at the *confidence*."**

*WAH! Waluigi has crossed nine borders in his professional life and can report that people look at the picture. People look at the picture first, last, and twice in between. Waluigi would also observe that a man who keeps two false identities in a locked cabinet in his own dining room has not prepared for an expedition. He has prepared for a departure.*

The hire picked one up, turned it over, and — the record has this from the hire himself, unprompted, offered as a confession rather than extracted — did not put it back. It went into his coat pocket while Wario was mid-sentence about tariffs, and it stayed there. Waluigi notes this without judgement. Everybody who has ever worked for Wario has taken something small, on the first day, as insurance. It is the closest thing to a pension the firm offers.

Then the boy asked the question.

**"The stories about that mountain,"** he said. **"People who go up don't come back. They fall down and they don't return. And there's supposed to be — things. Under it. Monsters."**

The room got quieter than a room with a grandfather clock in it can normally manage.

**"There are no monsters,"** Wario said.

He said it fast, and he said it loudly, and he said it while looking at the wall over the boy's shoulder rather than at the boy — three tells, in one sentence, from a man who has never successfully concealed anything in his life.

**"But the stories—"**

**"Stories are what poor people have instead of maps."** A hand slap on the table. Another plate went. **"Nobody falls. Nobody's under there. And if there IS anything under there it can take a number, because I am going to be *rich* and I don't have the schedule."**

*WAH! Note for the record that the man denying the existence of monsters under Mount Ebott went on to spend that same evening being hit in the face with a sharpened human femur by a small silent person on Mount Ebot. Waluigi does not believe in fate. Waluigi believes in invoicing, and the universe billed promptly.*

The last item of business was pay, and it took four minutes.

**"What's my cut?"** the boy asked.

**"Your cut."**

**"Of the treasure. If we find it."**

**"*When* we find it,"** Wario said, **"I take it. All of it. It's my expedition, my maps, my helicopter, my journal, my satellite images, my *idea*—"**

**"So what do I get?"**

**"Experience,"** said Wario. **"An adventure. A story for the grandkids. Do you know what people pay for an adventure?"**

**"Do I get *money*?"**

**"No."**

And that was the negotiation. The hire, according to the hire, said nothing further, put his hand in his coat pocket, and held on to the wallet he had already stolen for the rest of the conversation.
sections.waluigi_note: Two contracts were signed in that room and only one of them was spoken aloud. Wario offered a zero-share and considered the matter closed; the boy accepted the zero-share out loud and privately re-priced the job at one forged passport, payable immediately, taken in advance. Waluigi is not condoning theft. Waluigi is observing that Wario invented the terms, and that a wage of nothing produces employees who set their own. WAH.

sections.name: III. Antonio, Who Has a Family to Feed
sections.overview:
Then Wario ate.

There is no expedition in this archive, no crisis, no funeral and no fire, at which Wario has not at some point simply stopped and eaten, and the Ebot briefing broke for garlic bread roughly ninety seconds after the pay question was settled. He took a loaf off the map, tore it, and held half of it out across the table.

The hire reached for it. Wario's grip did not release.

**"Careful,"** he said, entirely pleasantly. **"Last guy grabbed too fast. I bit his hand."**

**"You bit—"**

**"Bit his hand. He was fine. He got a plaster and a story."**

The boy took the bread slowly, with the deliberate motion of a man withdrawing his fingers from a machine, and Wario laughed for some time and poured lemonade for both of them out of a jug so cold it was sweating on the map.

The chef came in with a second tray. Bald, aproned, unhurried, a hundred years of patience in the way he set things down: **Antonio**, who cooks in that villa and has apparently cooked in that villa for a considerable time.

**"He's the best,"** Wario announced. **"Best chef in the whole—"** a vague circle of the hand meaning the kingdom, the region, or the room **"—anywhere."**

**"Thank you, sir."**

**"What's he pay you?"** the boy asked.

Antonio's answer is recorded because the hire wrote it down that night, on the back of the stolen passport, and Waluigi has seen the handwriting.

**"Barely anything,"** Antonio said. **"But it is better than nothing, and I have a family to feed."**

Then he collected two plates from the floor, said nothing whatsoever about the third one in pieces by the plinth, and left.

*WAH! Waluigi wishes to place Antonio's sentence next to Wario's — "you get experience" — and leave the two of them touching on the page without further comment. That is the whole compensation policy of Wario's Enterprise, stated twice in one afternoon by both parties to it, and neither of them heard the other.*

Provisioning followed. Wario refused, in advance and at volume, to buy any named brand of anything.

**"High-end snacks are cardboard dipped in money,"** he said, from inside a cupboard. **"You pay for the *bag*. I don't eat bags."**

What he packed instead came out of a locked lower cabinet the boy had assumed was structural: the secret stash. Salted crackers in unmarked tins. Hard sausage. Dried fruit in wax paper. Two catering slabs of chocolate. Six loaves, wrapped for cold. Enough salt to preserve a horse. It was, and Waluigi will say this once, an entirely competent cold-weather ration list, assembled by a man who cannot spell the mountain but has genuinely never in his life been caught short of food.

**"Three weeks of this,"** Wario said, stacking it. **"Minimum. Nobody starves on my expeditions."**

Nobody has ever starved on a Wario expedition. They have frozen, fallen, been concussed, been sued, and been bitten by Wario. They have never gone hungry.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi has audited the villa's books and the line item marked KITCHEN is smaller than the line item marked GOLD LEAF, and Waluigi would like Antonio to know that this archive has noticed. The man is owed back-pay by any standard the Glazed Congress recognises. Waluigi will note also, since precision is the point of the exercise, that the ration planning for Ebot was better than the navigation, the aircraft, the personnel screening, and the objective combined. Wario prepares excellently for the parts of a disaster that involve lunch. WAH.

sections.name: IV. The Wariocopter Objection, and the Man on the Balcony
sections.overview:
The loading took the rest of the day and most of the night, and there was one argument in it worth filing.

The hire, looking at the aircraft on the villa's pad — a chartered grey thing with the livery half-scrubbed off and tape across the fuel gauge — asked the obvious question, which was why they were not taking the Wariocopter.

**"The Wariocopter,"** Wario said, **"is not for mountains."**

**"It flies."**

**"It flies *near the ground*. It's got one rotor and a lot of opinions and it burns fuel like a house fire. You put that thing at ten thousand feet in a crosswind and it comes apart like a wet biscuit and I am *inside it* when that happens."** He patted the charter's flank, which rang like a bin lid. **"This is a *proper* aircraft. Rented. Insured. Somebody else's."**

*WAH! Waluigi wishes it entered as a permanent finding of this archive that Wario declined to risk the Wariocopter on the grounds that it was fragile, expensive to run, and personally valuable to him, and then boarded a machine whose fuel gauge was covered with tape reading NOT ACCURATE, carrying an unbriefed twenty-two-year-old and, shortly, an abducted auditor. The Wariocopter was protected. The people were not.*

Crates went aboard: the rations, the coils of rope, a crate of climbing iron nobody had inspected, the oilcloth-wrapped map, six wrapped loaves, and the cold-weather kit. The hire loaded most of it, and at some point during the loading — his own account again — he took the stolen wallet out of his coat, where it had been sitting all afternoon against his ribs, and pushed it down into the bottom of his canvas kit-bag underneath a spare shirt, because coats get searched and bags get carried.

They lifted off before dawn with the courtyard lamps still on.

They were up for perhaps four minutes.

What happened next is the only part of the pre-flight period Waluigi can attest to personally, because Waluigi was in it. Waluigi was on his own balcony, eleven miles from the villa, at four o'clock in the morning, with a pair of binoculars.

He was not bird-watching.

He was watching a chartered aircraft with a scrubbed livery lift out of a villa he was not invited to, in the dark, carrying crates he had not been shown, and he was doing what he does, which is *making a note*. He had the aircraft's registration on the second page of the book. He was fourteen seconds from having its heading.

Then the landing lamp came round and found him standing there in a dressing gown with the binoculars up.

**"WALUIGI."**

The aircraft came down in the courtyard below — a courtyard Wario did not own, occupied by a chartered machine burning fuel that somebody had already been billed for — and Wario came up the thirty-one stairs two at a time.

**"You were *watching*."**

**"Waluigi was bird-watching."**

**"It's four in the morning."**

**"Owls,"** said Waluigi.

Wario took a double fistful of dressing gown, lifted him onto his toes, and put his face very close, and what he said is on the record because the hire heard all of it from the stairwell and repeated it twice, consistently:

**"I will smash your skull. I will smash it flat. I will put you in the ground and I will tell people you moved away."**

And then — because Wario cannot hold a threat and a plan in his head simultaneously, and because he had, as the archive will shortly establish, packed for this — he did not smash anything. He looked at Waluigi for a moment with an expression the hire described as *doing sums*, and then he went and got a sack.
sections.imageCaption: The chartered aircraft on the villa pad the night before departure, livery half-scrubbed and the fuel gauge taped. Wario's stated objection to the Wariocopter was that it flies near the ground. This flew high, once.
sections.waluigi_note: Everything about that balcony is worth an hour of anyone's time. Wario had spent an entire afternoon explaining that Waluigi could not be trusted with the plan, had checked behind a curtain for him, had broken a vase on the subject — and the instant he actually saw him he abducted him and took him along. Waluigi was excluded for being a security risk and then loaded aboard as cargo, which improved the security position not at all and improved the crew by exactly one competent person. WAH.

sections.name: V. The Sack Smelled of Onions
sections.overview:
The sack smelled of onions.

Everything above this point is reconstruction. Everything from here is Waluigi's, first-hand, and Waluigi would like the onions noted ahead of all of it — ahead of the mountain, ahead of the bones, ahead of the four dead names on the plank. Not a hood. Not a courier's dark bag. Not any of the respectable instruments of abduction a person of standing might reasonably expect to be carried off in. A produce sack. Forty-pound weave, stencilled in green on the outside, TOAD TOWN AGRICULTURAL BOARD — GRADE II, and smelling on the inside of onions and old rain.

**"Waluigi is awake,"** Waluigi said into the burlap.

**"I know,"** Wario said, and kept walking.

Thirty-one stairs. Waluigi counted them through Wario's shoulder, each one arriving in his ribs like a dropped brick, and at the bottom the air changed — cooler, wetter, carrying the flat chemical sweetness of rotor fuel and the particular smell of a courtyard that has been rained on all night and swept by nobody. Somewhere ahead of them a turbine was winding up in short unhappy coughs.

Here is the part the record will not show, so Waluigi will supply it. His left hand was free the entire time. It had been free since the landing of the fourteenth stair, when the drawstring slipped its knot against his glove. He could have been out of that sack, over the rail and three streets gone before Wario finished the flight of steps.

He stayed in the sack.

Not out of fear, which does not apply. Out of arithmetic. Wario had come at four in the morning with a rented aircraft already burning fuel on a courtyard he did not own, which meant somebody had been paid, which meant somebody expected a return, and Waluigi has learned that when Wario spends money in advance the day is going to become expensive for someone. Waluigi intended to be the person holding the receipt rather than the person written on it.

**"There is a mountain,"** Wario announced, to nobody, to the courtyard, to the wet flagstones. **"There is treasure in the mountain. There is a man who told me about the mountain and I only had to hit him once."**

*WAH! Observe the invoice already forming. One rented aircraft, one bribed informant, one punched informant — the same man, Waluigi later established, billed twice — and one abducted business partner transported as GRADE II produce. Waluigi has been called many things. He has never before been graded.*

The sack came off in the courtyard. Cold hit his face like a wet towel, and the rotor wash took his hat.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi wishes the archive to be precise about consent. He did not agree to the Ebot expedition; he declined to escape it, which is a different transaction and one Wario has never learned to tell apart. Every job the two of them have ever done runs on that confusion. Wario believes he wins arguments. What actually happens is that Waluigi decides the argument is cheaper to attend than to win, and files the difference. WAH.

sections.name: VI. Three Passengers, One of Whom Was Cheerful
sections.overview:
The aircraft was a Toad Town charter with the livery half-scrubbed off, a fat grey thing with a cracked chin-bubble and a strip of tape across the fuel gauge. Somebody had written **NOT ACCURATE** on the tape in grease pencil. Waluigi read it twice, which is two more times than the pilot ever did.

The pilot was a Toad in a flight jacket three sizes too generous, chewing something, headset already on. He did not ask who Waluigi was. He did not ask why one of his passengers had arrived in a vegetable sack. He held out a clipboard, Wario signed it with a thumbprint, and that was the entire boarding procedure of the Mount Ebot expedition.

The third passenger was already strapped into the rear bench with his knees up and a canvas kit-bag between his boots.

**"Jory,"** said the hire, putting a hand out into the noise. **"Jory Dobbs. We sort of met on the stairs just now. You were in the sack. I was holding the door."**

Waluigi looked at him. Twenty-something, cheap boots with good laces, a woollen hat, hands that would not stop moving over the buckles of a harness he had clearly never worn before. No visible weapon. No visible reason to be there. The single most breakable object on the aircraft, including the chin-bubble.

**"He answered an advertisement,"** Wario said, dropping into the seat opposite and making the whole airframe lean. **"Skilled labour. Very competitive rate."**

**"It's my first expedition,"** Dobbs said, brightly, to a man who had just been carried out of a building in a produce sack.

*WAH! An advertisement. Wario has hired a stranger off a public noticeboard the way other people buy a used shovel, and the stranger has arrived early, packed sandwiches, and is excited. Waluigi has seen this exact face before, on a young Toad who once volunteered to hold Wario's ladder. That Toad is now a story.*

Waluigi said nothing. He took the seat by the door, because the seat by the door is the seat by the door, and he buckled a harness that had been repaired with boot-lace, and he thought: *the boy will be hurt today.* Not a fear. A schedule. The only open question was which hour, and whether anyone competent would be standing near him when it happened.

The turbine climbed. The courtyard dropped away, wet and grey, and Toad Town rolled underneath them in a spread of chimney smoke and market awnings still folded shut against the dark.
sections.waluigi_note: Note the hiring standard, because it recurs. Wario does not recruit; he fills a seat. The kit-bag between Dobbs's boots contained sandwiches, a spare shirt, and no rope — and no one inspected it, because inspecting it would have meant admitting there was a list of things a person on this aircraft ought to be carrying. There was no list. There has never been a list. WAH.

sections.name: VII. The Exit Strategy, Discussed at Altitude
sections.overview:
Twenty minutes out of Toad Town, with the cabin dark and the Toad's instrument glow the only light in it, Waluigi asked the question he had been saving since the courtyard.

**"What is the plan for coming back?"**

Wario, eating, held up three fingers. **"Three weeks of food. And—"** he dug in a coat pocket and produced a black plastic lozenge with a rubber aerial and a single unlit lamp on it **"—*this*. GPS tracker. Broadcasts a position. Anything goes wrong, they come and get us."**

**"Who is *they*?"**

**"People. Rescue people. They exist, I've seen them on television."**

The hire, from the rear bench, said the useful thing. He said it quietly, and he said it into the noise, and he had to say it twice before anyone turned round.

**"A tracker tells them where you are. It doesn't dig you out. If we're under snow, they get a very accurate position for a hole in a mountain."**

*WAH! Waluigi would like it recorded that a twenty-two-year-old on his first expedition understood in four seconds the difference between being locatable and being rescuable, and that this understanding was, at that moment, the second most valuable thing on the aircraft after the fuel.*

**"Then don't get buried,"** Wario said, which is the Wario Method entire, in four words, and he has never improved on it.

**"A satellite phone,"** Waluigi said.

Wario chewed.

**"A satellite phone,"** Waluigi said again. **"So that the position comes with a *sentence* attached to it. So that the sentence can be *we are under six feet of snow on the north face, bring shovels* rather than a lamp blinking politely at a rescue service that has to guess."**

And Wario — and this is the single documented occasion in the whole eighteen hours, and Waluigi wishes it in bold — stopped chewing, thought about it, and said:

**"...Yeah. Yeah, alright. That's a good point. I should've got one of those."**

No shouting. No plate. He wrote it on the back of his hand with a grease pencil, where it presumably stayed until the first rain, which arrived approximately ninety minutes later.

*WAH! Enter it in the ledger. Wario conceded an oversight, out loud, unprompted, in front of two witnesses, at altitude. It changed nothing operationally — there was still no telephone — but Waluigi has audited this man for a decade and this is the only entry in that column.*

Then came the detail that Waluigi has not been able to put down since.

The hire, rummaging for the emergency kit, found the cold-weather bundles lashed under the rear bench and counted them out: three sets. Boots, thermals, an outer shell, mittens, a hat. And the third set was long. Absurdly long. Sleeves cut for arms that no Toad pilot and no twenty-two-year-old and certainly no Wario has ever possessed.

**"Whose are these?"**

**"They're spares,"** Wario said, too quickly, to the windscreen.

They were not spares. They had been ordered, and they had been packed, and they had been lashed down under a bench in an aircraft that departed a villa from which Waluigi had been deliberately and loudly excluded — hours before Wario stood in a stairwell in the dark pretending to be surprised to see him.

Waluigi did not say anything about it. Waluigi put his hand on the bundle in the dark, felt the length of the sleeve, and did the sum.
sections.waluigi_note: The trousers are the whole man. Wario told a room he was keeping Waluigi off this job, checked behind a curtain to be sure of it, broke a vase about it, and then packed thermal gear cut for a six-foot-four frame and loaded it aboard before dawn. He did not intend to invite Waluigi. He intended to *take* him, which in Wario's arithmetic is cheaper, because an invitation can be declined and a sack cannot. Waluigi's hand was free from the fourteenth stair and Waluigi already knew, by then, that there would be a coat in his size at the other end. Both men boarded that aircraft pretending to have been surprised. Neither of them was. WAH.

sections.name: VIII. The Weather Had an Opinion
sections.overview:
Forty minutes out the light went wrong.

Not dark — wrong. The grey ahead of them thickened into a wall the colour of a bruise, standing on the plain from cloud-base to ground, and the horizon simply stopped being a line. Rain arrived all at once, the way a bucket arrives, hammering the chin-bubble in sheets that turned the world into running glass.

**"That's weather,"** the pilot said over the intercom, in the tone of a man identifying a bird.

**"Go through it,"** Wario said.

**"That's not how—"**

**"Through it."**

The aircraft went through it.

Waluigi kept his eyes on the fuel tape. **NOT ACCURATE.** The needle behind it wandered a full quarter of the dial each time the airframe dropped, which told him nothing about the fuel and everything about how hard the machine was being shaken. Hail started, small and vicious, drumming the skin above their heads like someone throwing handfuls of gravel at a tin roof. The cabin lights browned out, came back, browned out.

Dobbs was grinning. That was the detail Waluigi could not get past. Both hands white on the bench-edge, boots braced, teeth showing — grinning, the way people grin on the first big drop of a ride they paid for.

**"Is it always like this?"** Dobbs shouted.

**"No,"** Waluigi said.

Wario was asleep. Genuinely, audibly asleep, chin on chest, arms folded over his stomach, riding out a hailstorm at three thousand feet with the serenity of a man who has never once considered that a thing he is inside of might stop working. Waluigi has spent years trying to decide whether that is courage or a missing organ. He has settled on the second and continues to be quietly, unforgivably jealous of it.

*WAH! Wario sleeps through hail. Waluigi does not sleep through hail, because Waluigi is the one who remembers that this aircraft has tape on its instruments and a signature made of thumb. One of us is at peace. One of us is correct. Historically these have never been the same person.*

Then the mountain came out of the rain on the left side, black and much too close, and the pilot said a word that the intercom clipped, and the world tipped.
sections.waluigi_note: The order of events matters more than the storm does. Wario gave the instruction to fly into the weather; the pilot began an objection; the objection was overridden by volume. Everything that follows in this filing — the crash, the boy's head, the bones, the bridge, the wasted day — descends from a two-word command issued by a man who was asleep ninety seconds later. WAH.

sections.name: IX. The Cave Took the Aircraft In
sections.overview:
There was a rock face, and then there was not.

The mountain opened — a black slot in the streaming stone, wide enough and no wider — and the pilot did the only intelligent thing anyone did all day, which was to stop fighting for the sky and steer for the hole. The rotors clipped something on the way in. The sound was enormous and short, a single *CLANG* like a church bell being hit with a church, and then they were inside, and the light went out, and the floor of the world came up.

They slid. That is the part nobody expects. The skids caught wet stone and the whole aircraft went along the cave floor sideways for what Waluigi later paced out as sixty-one feet, throwing up a rooster-tail of grit and sparks, the tail boom screaming along the wall until a boulder took it off. Then everything stopped, and the only sounds left were rain on the rock outside and the slow *tick, tick, tick* of hot metal starting to be cold metal.

Waluigi's harness had held. The boot-lace repair had held. Waluigi does not know who tied that knot, but he thinks about them fondly.

**"Everyone's fine,"** Wario announced, before checking.

The pilot was not fine. He was slumped forward in the straps with his headset knocked sideways and blood coming from his hairline in a slow, unhurried line, and when Waluigi got two fingers against his throat there was a pulse under them, steady and stupidly strong. Breathing. Out cold. A Toad's skull is a remarkable piece of engineering and Waluigi will hear no criticism of it.

Dobbs was on his hands and knees in the grit with his hat gone.

**"I'm okay,"** he said. **"I'm okay. I'm okay."**

He said it four more times. Waluigi crouched, took the boy's chin, and turned his face into the little light coming from the slot. Pupils the same size. Eyes tracking. A shine of blood above the left eyebrow where he had met a bracket, already welling, already running into the eye — scalp wounds bleed theatrically and mean almost nothing, but *almost* is doing heavy work in that sentence and Waluigi did not intend to test it.

Waluigi took out his glove-liner, folded it into a pad, put it in Dobbs's own hand and closed the boy's fingers over it.

**"Press,"** he said. **"You. Not Waluigi. Keep pressing until Waluigi says."**

Giving a frightened person a job is not kindness. It is load management. A man holding a bandage to his own head is a man who is not screaming, not standing up too fast, and not wandering into a dark cave to be helpful.

*WAH! Note who checked the pilot. Note who checked the boy. Note who announced that everyone was fine from a seated position with his eyes still shut. Waluigi has decided not to be bitter about this, and has instead decided to write it down, which is worse.*
sections.imageCaption: The slot, the scree, and sixty-one feet of gouge in wet gravel, with the tail boom lying where the boulder took it off. The pilot's decision to stop fighting for the sky and steer for the hole is the only manoeuvre in this file the archive rates as correct.
sections.waluigi_note: Two casualties inside four seconds and neither of them was the man who caused the crash — this is the standing pattern of every Wario operation in the archive, and the reason Waluigi keeps a folded glove-liner in a pocket he never mentions. The pilot was breathing throughout. Waluigi checked him again at every re-entry to the cave. Nobody asked him to. WAH.

sections.name: X. The Rope Chain
sections.overview:
The slot the aircraft had come through was thirty feet above the cave floor and forty feet back, up a slope of loose scree that moved when you looked at it. Everything they owned was down at the wreck. Everything they needed was going to be up on the mountain.

Wario's plan was to carry it all himself in one trip. Wario's plan is always to carry it all himself in one trip.

He got eleven feet. The scree went out from under him like a dropped tray and he came back down in an avalanche of rock, a crate, two coils of line and one canteen, landing on the crate, which lost.

**"The mountain is cheating,"** Wario said, from the floor.

Waluigi did not laugh. Waluigi went and got the rope.

What they built took an hour and it worked, and Waluigi would like the archive to show that it was not complicated, because the useful things never are. Three stations. Dobbs at the bottom on the flat, with the glove-liner taped to his head and one job: fill the net, tie the net, shout. Waluigi in the middle at the pinch of the scree, braced in a rock cleft with the line over his shoulder and around his back — the ugly, unglamorous body-belay that every climbing manual describes and nobody in Wario's employ has ever read. Wario at the top in the slot, where the only requirement was to pull very hard for a long time, which is the one athletic event in which Wario is genuinely world-class.

**"Net's up!"** from below.

*Haul. Clip. Slap the rope twice. Wait for two slaps back.*

**"Net's up!"**

Nine loads. Rations, line, lamps, the good crowbar, the bad crowbar, Wario's personal crate of things Wario will not discuss, and last of all the aircraft's own emergency kit, which Waluigi took off its bracket without mentioning to anyone, because a man who has been in one crash that day may reasonably plan for two.

Two slaps. Two slaps back. The rope creaked over Waluigi's shoulder and the wet stone of the cleft pressed a cold bar across his spine, and up in the slot Wario hauled and swore and hauled, and down on the flat a bleeding boy tied knots he had learned forty minutes earlier and tied them *correctly*, every time, checking each one twice before he shouted.

*Waluigi noticed that. Waluigi noticed the checking.*

That was the last good hour of the day. Three people, one rope, a system that held. Waluigi will take it out and look at it later, when he needs to remember that the arrangement is capable of working.
sections.waluigi_note: The rope chain is the only part of this expedition Waluigi would repeat unchanged. It worked because for one hour nobody was in charge of it — each station could see what the next station needed, and the signal was two slaps on a line rather than a shouted order down a cave. Wario has been trying to give instructions his whole life and has never once produced an hour as clean as the one where he was simply the heaviest available counterweight. WAH.

sections.name: XI. The Small One Who Threw
sections.overview:
It was standing on the scree above the slot when they came out into the rain, and it had been standing there long enough to be wet.

Four feet tall, perhaps a little less. A shape rather than a face — a hood or a helm, Waluigi could not resolve which even at twenty feet, with nothing under the brim of it but shadow that did not lighten when the sky did. No breath in the cold air. Waluigi checked for breath. There was none.

**"Hello!"** Wario bellowed, in the voice of a man greeting a barrel of coins. **"We are surveyors!"**

It threw the bone.

No windup, no shift of weight — the arm simply moved through the throw and the bone was already gone, a white blur that went past Wario's ear and struck the rock behind him with a *crack* like a snapped floorboard. It was a femur. It was old, and dry, and it had been sharpened at one end.

Wario charged. Of course Wario charged. Twenty-two stone of yellow enthusiasm went up that scree slope with a crowbar raised, and the small figure watched him come, and when the crowbar arrived the figure was not there.

There was no leap. Waluigi was watching for the leap. Waluigi has fought things that jump, things that blink, things that stand behind you and pretend they were always behind you, and he knows what all of them look like at the moment of departure. This one simply stopped occupying its position — a soft *whump* of air folding into the hole where a body had been, a smell like a struck match, and then it was eleven feet to the left and slightly downhill, arm already through another throw.

The second bone hit Wario in the back of the head. He went down on his knees, said a word about the mountain's mother, and got up.

The third missed Dobbs by the width of a decision, because Waluigi had already taken two long steps and put himself in the line, and the bone went into the scree beside his boot hard enough to bury half its length.

Waluigi's hands were up and glowing before he decided to raise them. Ice does not miss a thing that teleports — you do not aim at where it is, you aim at where it will need to stand — and Waluigi had already worked out that the small one always arrived on flat footing, always, never on the loose slope.

He froze the flat footing. Every patch of it inside thirty feet, in one long sweeping arc, until the scree glittered like a shattered window.

The small one reappeared, skidded, went down on one knee for exactly as long as it takes to be surprised, and then was gone — not eleven feet this time, but entirely, the air closing over the space with that same soft *whump* and the same smell of a struck match.

*WAH! It did not speak. Not one word, not a hiss, not a laugh. Waluigi has been threatened by professionals on four planes of existence and every single one of them monologued. Silence is not menace, whatever the poets say. Silence is a job. That thing was working a shift.*

It did not come back. Wario declared victory. Waluigi looked at the femur standing out of the scree by his boot, sharpened, dry, human-sized, and did not touch it, and did not mention what the sharpening implied, because Dobbs was eleven feet away and had gone very quiet at last.
sections.waluigi_note: Three facts, filed apart from the fight. One: the thing threw bones it did not bring, which means the bones were already on the mountain. Two: it never chose the same footing twice, which is the behaviour of something that has been hurt on that slope before. Three: it broke off the moment the ground stopped being reliable, rather than the moment it started losing. That is not a beast. That is a sentry with orders and an exit. WAH.

sections.name: XII. The Ground Gave Up Its Property
sections.overview:
The shaking started under the boots first, a fine buzz through the soles like standing on a bridge with a cart crossing it, and then the whole slope was moving and the rain was going sideways and the noise came up out of the rock — a long low grinding, not thunder, nothing in the sky at all.

**"DOWN!"** Waluigi shouted, and got a fistful of Dobbs's collar and put him flat against the lee of a boulder, and lay across him, which the boy will remember and Waluigi will deny.

Wario stayed standing. Wario tried to stand *harder*. It is Waluigi's considered view that Wario believed the earthquake could be resisted through effort and was preparing to win.

The slope opened in long thin seams, a foot wide at most, running downhill in three parallel lines like a rake dragged through wet clay. And out of the seams came the bones.

Not thrown. Not tumbled. *Rising* — pushed up the way a splinter is pushed out of a healing hand, unhurried, arriving out of the wet earth by the hundred. Ribs. Long bones. A jaw with three teeth in it. They came up through the mud and they lay there in the rain, gleaming, and the grinding stopped, and the shaking stopped, and the mountain went quiet with all its property laid out on the surface where anyone could count it.

Waluigi counted anyway. Forty-one visible from where he lay, in a strip of ground the size of a market stall.

He got up. He helped Dobbs up. The boy's hands were shaking and the glove-liner had come loose and there was fresh blood down the side of his face and he was staring at the jaw with the three teeth.

**"Are those—"**

**"Yes."**

**"How many people—"**

**"Do not,"** Waluigi said, **"count them."**

Wario was already picking one up and testing it against his palm for weight.

*WAH! Wario has found a free club. Waluigi wishes to state for the record that the free club was recently a person, that the mountain has just handed us the results of every previous expedition, and that the correct response to a hillside politely returning its dead is to go home, wash, and take up an indoor profession.*

Waluigi looked back down the slope at the black slot where the aircraft lay ticking in the dark, and did the arithmetic he had been avoiding since the crash: no radio, no fuel certainty, one unconscious pilot, one concussed boy, and now a slope that produced skeletons on request. Every number said turn around.

He turned uphill. Waluigi would like it recorded that he knows exactly how stupid that was, and that he did it because the boy could not walk back down the scree alone and Wario was not going to notice for another two hours that anyone was missing.
sections.waluigi_note: The seams ran parallel and downhill, evenly spaced, and the bones came up through them along their whole length at once. Waluigi does not know what that is. He knows what it is *not*: it is not a landslide exposing a grave, because a landslide moves the ground sideways and this ground opened in lines and stayed put. Somebody or something on this mountain buries in rows. WAH.

sections.name: XIII. The Bridge That Had Been Improved
sections.overview:
The gorge was ninety feet across and the bridge was a good one — cut stone, mortared, with a low parapet and drainage channels, the kind of thing an empire builds when it expects to still be there in a century. Somebody had improved it afterwards.

Waluigi stopped at the abutment and did not step on it, and put his arm out flat in front of Dobbs, and said nothing for a while.

The improvements were these. Along both parapets, at knee height and shin height, ran slots — clean, machined, no wider than a coin, spaced a stride apart the whole length. In the slots, at the near end where the rain had washed the grime away, the dull grey edges of razors, angled to catch a leg going forward. Beneath the deck, at intervals, brass nozzles the diameter of a thumb, pointing up and inward, their throats black with old soot and stinking faintly of lamp oil even in the downpour. And on the deck itself, six stone plates a shade paler than the rest of the stonework, each one set a fraction low.

**"It's a bridge,"** Wario said.

**"It is a machine,"** Waluigi said. **"It is a machine for turning people into a report."**

Wario walked onto it.

Waluigi has thought a great deal about that step. There was no argument, no bravado, no moment where Wario weighed the razors against the treasure. He simply did not believe the bridge applied to him, in the same way he does not believe stairs are tiring, and he went out onto the deck of it at his usual bulldozing pace, and by the purest and most infuriating luck his first three strides landed between the pale plates.

His fourth landed on one.

The plate went down half an inch with a sound like a jar of pickles opening in the next room. Then the whole bridge spoke at once: a *shing* of steel coming out of stone as sixty razors extended from the parapets in a rolling wave, and behind it the *whump* of the nozzles lighting — six gouts of flame standing straight up off the deck, one after another down the length of the span, orange in the rain, roaring.

Wario ran. There is nothing else in the record. Twenty-two stone of him went down that bridge through fire with his arms over his face, took a razor across the thigh, took another across the same thigh going the other way, and came off the far abutment on fire in three places and rolling in the mud with a great deal of commentary.

The flames died. The razors withdrew. The bridge reset itself with a series of small precise clicks and lay there in the rain looking like a bridge.

**"COME ON!"** Wario shouted from the far side. **"IT'S FINE!"**

Waluigi knelt at the near abutment and put his palm on the first pale plate and pressed. Nothing. He pressed harder. Nothing. He stood on it with his whole weight and it did not move.

*WAH! Weight. It is graded by weight, and Wario is the only object in this expedition heavy enough to qualify. Sixty razors and six flame jets, and the bridge looked at Waluigi and declined to consider him a person. Waluigi has never before been insulted by masonry and he intends to hold a grudge against this specific bridge for the remainder of his natural life.*

They crossed behind Wario's footprints — Waluigi first, Dobbs's fist knotted in his belt, both of them stepping where a burning man had already proved the stone was safe.
sections.imageCaption: The improved bridge. Machined slots at knee and shin height, razors angled to catch a leg going forward, wire below. An empire built the crossing; something else finished it.
sections.waluigi_note: The trap is the strongest evidence on the mountain and everyone walked past it. Razors, oil-fed jets, pressure plates on a graded threshold, and a reset — that is maintained equipment. Someone oils those nozzles. Someone replaces those blades. And the threshold is set high enough to ignore a child, which means whoever built it was not trying to keep out the small silent thing that throws bones. It was built to stop something much larger, and it is still being serviced. WAH.

sections.name: XIV. Four Names on a Plank
sections.overview:
The sign stood past the bridge where the path bent around a shoulder of rock, and it had been made with care by someone with no talent for it.

A plank, a hand's width thick, weathered silver, bolted to two iron stakes driven deep. The lettering was burned in rather than painted — a hot iron, worked slowly, the strokes wobbling where the hand had got tired. Rain ran off the top edge in a steady bead and dripped onto the words.

> **RIP — 4 MISSING HUMANS.** JAVIER. MIKAELA. DANIEL. And, fourth, a name burned in like the others and then greyed almost out of the wood: **PRINCE ALPHONSE.**

Three names clean. The fourth had been gone over — not scratched out in anger but rubbed, repeatedly, with something soft and greasy, until the burned grooves had filled with grey and the letters had to be read at an angle against the light. Waluigi found the angle. Waluigi always finds the angle.

**"Prince Alphonse,"** he said aloud.

Dobbs leaned in with his good eye. **"Who's Prince Alphonse?"**

**"Prince of the Greeks,"** Waluigi said. **"Three hundred and ninety-two to four hundred and thirty-two."**

There was a pause exactly long enough for a young man with a head wound to do subtraction.

**"That's— wait. That's backwards. That's forty years the wrong way."**

**"Yes."**

**"So he was born after he died?"**

**"Yes,"** Waluigi said. **"BC counts down. Waluigi did not design the calendar and refuses to apologise for it."**

Wario, who had lost interest at the word *Greeks*, was already prying at the bolts to see whether the stakes were worth anything.

The smudging is what Waluigi could not put down. Three names left legible, one worked at until it nearly went away, and all four on the same plank in the same hand. Nobody burns a name into wood at that cost and then removes it for tidiness. Either somebody wanted the prince forgotten and could not bring themselves to take the plank down, or somebody wanted him remembered privately, by the small number of people who would know to tilt their head against the light.

*WAH! Four missing, and one of them has been buffed. Waluigi has audited enough ledgers to know what a partially erased line item means: the person holding the pen was frightened of exactly one of the entries. Not all four. One.*

Waluigi wrote all four names in his book, tilted the page out of the rain, and drew a small square around the fourth.

The page is filed as [[prop:prop_ebot_summit_plank|the plank, as copied]].
sections.imageCaption: The memorial plank: three names burned clean, and PRINCE ALPHONSE rubbed grey by a hand that came back to do it. Nobody burns a name into wood at that cost and then removes it for tidiness.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi is not asserting that a Greek prince died on this mountain, and he is certainly not asserting the dates, which are impossible in the direction that matters. He is asserting that a plank exists, that it is bolted to iron stakes at some effort, that it names four humans as missing rather than dead, and that the fourth name was worked over by a patient hand with a greasy rag. Three of those four names are recoverable. Someone should go and recover them before the mountain finishes the job. WAH.

sections.name: XV. What Waluigi Told the Boy Under the Overhang
sections.overview:
They sheltered under a lip of rock while Wario went ahead to shout at some scenery, and Waluigi re-dressed the head wound, and Dobbs — because he was young, and because talking is what a frightened person does with the part of himself that is still working — asked why anyone would put a sign up on a mountain nobody comes to.

So Waluigi told him. Two fingers holding the pad, one hand paying out a strip of linen, rain sheeting off the overhang in front of them like a beaded curtain.

**"Because of the Treaty,"** Waluigi said. **"The Mushroom Treaty. Signed after the Chaos Heart business, when everybody had finally frightened themselves enough to sit in a room. One line of it says that a party going into unmapped ground leaves a marker with the names of anybody it loses. That is all a marker like that is. Somebody obeyed the paperwork on a hillside in the rain."**

**"Somebody rubbed a name off it, though."**

**"Yes,"** Waluigi said. **"That part is not in the Treaty."**

He tied the linen off. It was not a good bandage. It was the second-best bandage available with wet hands and no light, which is a different and more honest standard.

**"The Treaty is why the Glazed Congress happens,"** he went on, because the boy's eyes were tracking and he wanted them to keep tracking. **"Fifteen delegations in a hall, once a year, arguing about roads. The first one was in Beanbean. Waluigi was there. Waluigi wore a hat that three separate delegates tried to have removed from the room, and Waluigi's hat outlasted all three of them."**

**"You were at the Glazed Congress?"**

**"Waluigi is in the founding portrait. Back row. Slightly too tall."**

The rain went on. Dobbs asked what the Congress was *for*, and Waluigi found he had to go further back than he meant to — to the Great Migration, when whole peoples walked west along roads that no longer exist because the ground they crossed does not exist either; and from there, unavoidably, to the shape of the world, which Waluigi delivered flatly, holding a wet strip of linen, to a bleeding twenty-year-old under a rock.

**"The world is a doughnut,"** Waluigi said. **"There is a hole. Something took a bite out of the far side of it. When people say the Migration was a journey, what they mean is that the land those people were standing on stopped being there, and they walked until it started again."**

Dobbs was quiet a moment. **"Is that true?"**

**"Waluigi has been told it by a god, a Jester, and Wario,"** Waluigi said. **"Two of the three had nothing to gain."**

*Waluigi will admit something here that he would not admit aloud. He did not tell the boy the shape of the world for the boy's benefit. He told him because the boy was going grey around the mouth and needed a voice to hold onto, and because the only thing Waluigi has ever had in quantity is things to say. It worked. The colour came back. Waluigi files this under first aid.*

Wario came back around the shoulder of rock at that point and asked whether they were going to sit in a hole all day like a family of moles, and the lecture ended, and the boy stood up on his own, which he had not been able to do twenty minutes earlier.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi taught a concussed man the shape of the planet to keep him conscious, and it is the single most useful thing anyone did on the mountain after the rope chain. Talk is a stimulant. A person answering questions is a person whose skull is still working, and you find out the instant it stops. Wario's method of monitoring the boy was to periodically shout his name and accept silence as agreement. WAH.

sections.name: XVI. The Northern War, According to a Man Who Was Not In It
sections.overview:
The last thousand feet were a staircase.

Not a metaphor — a staircase, cut into the rock, two hundred and some steps of it, each tread worn into a shallow dish by feet that had gone up and down it long enough to wear stone. Waluigi counted the dished treads and stopped counting at ninety, because ninety dished treads is already a number that means centuries of traffic on a mountain that was supposed to be empty.

Wario talked the entire way up. Wario talks when he climbs; it is how he refuses to admit he is out of breath.

**"This is Northern War stone,"** he announced, slapping a wall. **"You can tell. The Northern War, that's where the money went. Everybody buried everything. My cousin's cousin knew a man who dug up a strongbox the size of a cart."**

**"Which side,"** Waluigi said.

**"What?"**

**"Of the Northern War. Which side buried the strongbox."**

**"The rich one,"** Wario said, with total confidence, and kept climbing.

The Northern War is the war that everyone in a tavern has an uncle in and nobody can put a date on. Waluigi has now heard it described as forty years long, as a single winter, as a dispute over a river, and as the reason the Migration happened, which is chronologically impossible in at least two of those versions. It is not history. It is the shape people press their losses into. Every abandoned fort with good stonework gets assigned to it, and every hole in a ledger, and every hillside anybody is frightened of.

*WAH! Wario has identified the age of a staircase by hitting it. Waluigi wishes to note that the same man, four hours earlier, identified a hailstorm as 'fine' and a bridge full of razors as 'a bridge.' His instrument is confidence and it has never once been calibrated.*

But the steps were real, and the wear on them was real, and somewhere near the top Waluigi passed a place where the rock beside the staircase had been squared off flat and a niche cut into it, empty now, the size of a lamp or a small statue or an offering bowl. Rain had made a little pool in the bottom of it. Around the rim, worn nearly out, ran a line of cut letters in an alphabet Waluigi does not read, and one shape he did recognise, because it appears at the head of every treaty-era survey marker between here and the Regal frontier: a mason's index mark.

He copied it into his book. He did not mention it. Wario was ahead by then, and Wario was shouting that he could see the top.
sections.waluigi_note: Two dating claims went up that staircase and only one of them can be checked. Wario's Northern War is a tavern noun that expands to cover any old stone. The niche is different: it carries a survey index mark of a type Waluigi has seen on treaty-era boundary stones, which means an official party stood on this staircase with the authority to cut marks into it. Someone surveyed this mountain. That fact becomes extremely funny in about forty minutes. WAH.

sections.name: XVII. One T
sections.overview:
There was no treasure at the top. There was a cairn, a view of grey rain in every direction, and a second plank.

This one was smaller and older and had been nailed to a post rather than bolted, and it had been made by the same trade as the first — burned lettering, tired strokes — and it said:

> **MOUNT EBOT — SUMMIT — 1,340 FT — NO FURTHER SERVICE**

Waluigi read it. Waluigi read it again. Then Waluigi went very still in a way that Dobbs apparently found more alarming than the bridge.

**"Give Waluigi the map."**

**"The map is fine,"** Wario said.

**"Give Waluigi the map."**

The map came out of the crate wrapped in oilcloth, which is the single competent piece of expedition practice Wario has ever demonstrated and Waluigi will not be mentioning it again. He opened it on the flat of the cairn with the rain pattering on it and put his thumb on the mountain they were standing on.

**MOUNT EBOT.** One T.

Bottom right corner, in a neat oval cartouche with a compass rose in it: **THE OLD WORLD MAPPING COMPANY — SURVEY SERIES IV — CORRECTIONS ON APPLICATION.**

The sheet is in the archive. Waluigi has filed it as [[prop:prop_ebot_survey_iv|Survey Series IV, Sheet 41]], and the reader is invited to put a thumb on the same mountain and count the letters.

**"Mount Ebott,"** Waluigi said, **"has two."**

**"Same thing."**

**"It is not the same thing. Mount Ebott is four hundred miles east and it is full of monsters and a barrier and a king with a beard. This is Mount Ebot. Mount Ebot is full of *bones*, and a *bridge*, and *no treasure whatsoever*."**

**"Same *thing*,"** Wario said, louder, which is what Wario does with a fact instead of accepting it.

And there it was, the whole day, laid out on wet paper under a thumb. A Mapping Company clerk somewhere had set the type for *Ebott*, dropped a T, and printed it — and the printed error had gone out into the world and been bought, and folded, and trusted, and eventually handed to a man who had punched an informant for directions and could not read either way. Every single thing that had happened since four o'clock that morning had happened because of one absent letter.

**"So we climbed the wrong mountain,"** Dobbs said. He had blood dried down one side of his face and he was starting, very quietly, to laugh, and it was not entirely a well laugh.

**"We climbed the wrong mountain,"** Waluigi agreed.

*WAH! Waluigi has been abducted in a produce sack, hailed on, crashed, shot at with a dead man's leg, offered a hillside of skeletons, declined personhood by a bridge, and marched up two hundred dished steps in the rain — and the responsible party is a compositor with cold hands in a printing house that no longer exists. Waluigi wants the cartouche. Waluigi wants the clerk's name. Waluigi wants CORRECTIONS ON APPLICATION and Waluigi intends to apply.*

Wario kicked the cairn. The cairn, which had been there a long time and had opinions about weather, did not react. Then he sat down on it, in the rain, at the top of the wrong mountain, and said the only thing he said all day that Waluigi has been unable to argue with.

**"Well,"** Wario said. **"It was still a mountain."**
sections.imageCaption: The summit plank, and the spelling that cost the expedition everything: MOUNT EBOT — SUMMIT — 1,340 FT — NO FURTHER SERVICE. One T. Mount Ebott, four hundred miles east, has two.
sections.waluigi_note: The error is upstream of everybody. Wario did not misread the map; the map was wrong, and the map carried a survey house's cartouche, a series number, and an invitation to file corrections — the full costume of an authority. That is the whole finding of this expedition: a survey house's typographical slip travelled four hundred miles and a fortnight and arrived as a helicopter, a crash, a head wound and four names on a plank. Nobody on this mountain made a mistake today except a man setting type fifty years ago. WAH.

sections.name: XVIII. The Descent, and Who Actually Started the Aircraft
sections.overview:
Going down took two hours and cost nothing, because going down never does until it does. They crossed the bridge on Wario's scorch marks. The slope with the seams in it had closed, and the bones were gone — not covered, *gone*, with the mud smooth over the seams and not one rib left on the surface. Waluigi walked that strip twice looking for the jaw with three teeth. He did not find it. He has decided not to think about that at night.

The small silent one did not come back. Waluigi kept his hands out of his pockets the whole way down regardless.

The aircraft was where they had left it, tail-boom gone, one skid folded, sitting nose-down in the grit of the cave with rain blowing in through the slot and the pilot still strapped in and still, thank every calendar saint, breathing.

Wario's plan for extraction was to walk. Ninety miles. In the rain. Carrying a Toad.

**"Or,"** Waluigi said, **"Waluigi could start the aircraft."**

**"You can't fly."**

**"Waluigi did not say fly. Waluigi said *start*."**

He had watched the boarding, because Waluigi watches everything, and a rented Toad Town charter is not a complicated machine — battery master, fuel valve, throttle to the detent, starter, and then a great deal of noise and a decision. He got into the right-hand seat with his knees against the cracked chin-bubble and went through it in order, out loud, so that Dobbs could hear a person being calm.

The turbine caught on the third attempt. The sound of it in a stone cave was physically painful and the most beautiful thing Waluigi had heard in eleven hours.

The noise is what woke the pilot. Not the smelling salts from the emergency kit Waluigi had taken off the bracket that morning — though Waluigi used those too, and would like both facts in the record — but his own engine turning over without him. He came up out of the straps swearing, took one look at the tall man in his right-hand seat with a hand on his throttle, and swore differently.

**"Off,"** the pilot said. **"Off, off, off — hands *off* —"**

**"With pleasure,"** Waluigi said, and got out of the seat, and helped the man's headset onto his bleeding head, and then went back to strap a semi-conscious twenty-year-old into a bench with a boot-lace harness.

They flew out through the slot on the second attempt, scraping something on the way, into a sky that had finished raining hours ago on the other side of the mountain. Behind them Mount Ebot stood up out of the cloud with its staircase and its bridge and its plank and its four names, one of them rubbed nearly out.

Wario slept the whole way home.
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi would like the extraction attributed correctly, since no one else will do it. He took the emergency kit off its bracket before the first climb, kept the pilot's airway clear at three separate check-ins, started the aircraft, woke the pilot with his own engine, and handed the controls straight back to the only person qualified to hold them. Wario's contribution to the extraction phase was to propose walking ninety miles with an unconscious Toad over one shoulder, and then to fall asleep. WAH.

aftermath:
## Aftermath & Operational Standing

**1. Operational result.** Nothing was recovered. No treasure existed, because no treasure was ever alleged to exist on this mountain by anyone; the claim attached to Mount Ebott, four hundred miles east, and arrived at Mount Ebot through a printing error. The expedition's total material gain was one misprinted chart, retained by Waluigi as evidence, and one sharpened femur, retained by Wario as a club.

**2. Casualties.** The charter pilot — a Toad, name withheld pending his own account — took a head laceration and roughly nine hours of unconsciousness in the crash, and flew his own aircraft out under his own hands the same evening. Jory Dobbs sustained a scalp wound above the left eye, bled heavily, remained oriented throughout, and was walking unaided by nightfall; Waluigi recommends he be looked at by somebody with a lamp. Wario sustained two razor cuts to the same thigh and burns to three places, and declined treatment on the grounds that it was still raining.

**3. Materiel.** The charter lost its tail boom, one skid, and its right rotor tip; the operator's bill has not yet reached Waluigi and Waluigi intends to be elsewhere when it does. The aircraft emergency kit was removed from its bracket before the climb and used on Salam.

**4. Exposure.** Three parties on the mountain now know that a Wario expedition can be put on a slope by a printed error: whatever posted the sentry, whoever services the bridge, and the Old World Mapping Company, if it still exists in any form that can be served with a correction notice. Four names remain on a plank past the bridge. Three of them are legible.

**5. Compensation.** None was agreed and none was paid. The hire's share of the proceeds was set at the briefing, in front of a witness, at nothing — the offered consideration was **"experience, an adventure, a story for the grandkids."** He is owed nothing under the terms he accepted and everything under any other standard the Glazed Congress recognises, and Waluigi notes that the villa's kitchen staff are on comparable terms. Antonio, who cooks in that building, describes his own wage as **"barely anything, but better than nothing, and I have a family to feed."**

**6. Documents in circulation.** Two forged identity documents were produced at the briefing in the names **GREGORIO MORETTI** ([[prop:prop_ebot_passport|reproduced here]]) and **HANS KÜBLER**, with photographs matching nobody present. One remains in Wario's cabinet. The other left the villa in the hire's coat pocket and is, at time of filing, in the bottom of a canvas kit-bag under a spare shirt. Waluigi declines to recover it and declines to explain why.

**7. Equipment not carried.** No satellite phone. The extraction plan consisted of three weeks' rations and one GPS tracker, and the flaw in it — that a tracker reports a position but does not dig anybody out from under snow — was identified aloud by the hire in the cabin and conceded by Wario, who wrote *phone* on the back of his own hand in grease pencil and then flew into rain. The cold-weather kit did include a full thermal set cut for a six-foot-four frame, lashed under the rear bench before departure, for a passenger who had not been invited.

**8. Eight years on.** This filing sat in a crate. The [[prop:prop_ebot_correction_demand|correction demand]] was posted, acknowledged by a clerk, and never answered; the Old World Mapping Company burned down some years afterwards with its plates inside, which means Survey Series IV can no longer be corrected by anybody at any price. Every sheet still in circulation still says Mount Ebot with one T, and every sheet still in circulation is still wrong in exactly the way that put a twenty-two-year-old on a staircase with his scalp open. Waluigi releases the record now because a hazard that cannot be corrected can at least be published.
waluigiAssessment:
## Waluigi's Assessment & Editorial Verdict

**1. The letter did the damage, not the mountain.** Waluigi has audited disasters caused by greed, by cowardice, by vampires, and by architecture, and this is the first one caused by typesetting. A clerk at the Old World Mapping Company dropped a T out of *Ebott*, the plate went to press, the press went to market, the market sold it to a man who punches informants for directions, and eighteen hours later a twenty-year-old was bleeding into his own eye on a staircase four hundred miles from the mountain he had been hired to climb. Every wound in this filing has that clerk's fingerprint on it. The chart's own cartouche says CORRECTIONS ON APPLICATION. Waluigi has applied. Waluigi will keep applying.

**2. The bridge is the real intelligence and everybody walked past it.** Sixty razors seated in machined slots, six oil-fed jets with sooted throats, six pressure plates graded so that a man of ordinary build does not trigger them, and a full reset after firing. Blades that clean do not survive a decade of weather untended and lamp oil does not refill itself. Somebody maintains that span *now*. Whoever they are, they set the threshold heavy — heavy enough to ignore Waluigi, heavy enough to ignore the small silent thing that throws bones. The bridge is not guarding the summit against climbers. It is guarding something against something bigger than us, and it is winning, and no one has told it the war is over.

**3. The sentry was working, not hunting.** It threw three bones and withdrew the instant the footing became unreliable. It never repeated a landing spot. It made no sound whatsoever — no threat, no cry, nothing — and it took no trophy and pursued no one down the slope. Waluigi has been menaced by professionals across four planes and every one of them talked. That thing had a post and an exit and it used both. Someone or something on Mount Ebot keeps a rota.

**4. The ground buries in rows.** The seams that opened in the earthquake ran parallel, evenly spaced, downhill, and the bones came up along their whole length at once. By the descent, the seams had closed and the surface was smooth and not one bone remained. Whatever administrates that hillside puts its dead in lines and takes them back in under six hours. Waluigi counted forty-one bones in a strip the size of a market stall and stopped counting on purpose.

**5. The plank was rubbed, not scratched.** Javier, Mikaela and Daniel are burned clean into the wood. The fourth name — read against the light, at an angle — is Prince Alphonse, and it has been worked over patiently with something soft and greasy by a hand that never once considered simply taking the plank down. Waluigi offers no opinion on the dates he recited on the mountain and asks that the archive stop quoting them at him. He offers a firm opinion on the smudging: a partially erased line item means the person holding the pen was afraid of exactly one of the entries.

**6. The rope chain worked because nobody commanded it.** Three stations, one line, two slaps up and two slaps back — the single hour of this expedition Waluigi would repeat without changing a comma. It worked because each station could see what the next one needed, and because Wario's role was reduced to being the heaviest available counterweight, which is the role in which he has never yet failed anyone.

**7. The trousers are the confession.** Wario spent an afternoon telling a room that Waluigi could not be trusted with this job. He checked behind a curtain. He broke a vase on the subject. And then he ordered thermal gear cut for a six-foot-four frame, packed it, lashed it under the rear bench, and flew it out of the villa hours before he pretended to be surprised by a man on a balcony with binoculars. Waluigi was never excluded from the Ebot expedition. Waluigi was *scheduled* for it, in the one way Wario finds cheaper than asking, because an invitation can be declined and a sack cannot. Waluigi's hand was free from the fourteenth stair and stayed in the sack anyway, so let the record show that both men boarded that aircraft performing a surprise neither of them felt.

**8. The wage produced the theft, in that order.** A man was offered nothing for eighteen hours of work that included a head wound, and he took a forged passport off a table before the offer was even made — which means he had already read the room correctly. Waluigi is not the ethics board. Waluigi is the auditor, and the audit finding is that Wario's compensation policy is a system for converting employees into creditors who collect in kind. Antonio in the kitchen has taken the same deal and settled for less.

**9. The one conceded point.** In ten years of filings this archive contains exactly one instance of Wario hearing an objection, considering it, and saying *that's a good point* — and it was a twenty-two-year-old on his first job explaining that a GPS tracker is a locator and not a shovel. It changed nothing. There was still no telephone on the mountain. But it is the only entry in that column and Waluigi wants it preserved before Wario denies it.

**RECOMMENDATION.** File a correction demand against the Old World Mapping Company under the survey-marker clause of the Mushroom Treaty, attach the chart, and require the plate reprinted with both Ts and a rider naming Mount Ebot separately with its bridge, its sentry, and its four missing humans. Until that plate is corrected, every party that buys Survey Series IV is buying this day. Waluigi has already lived it once and declines the anniversary. WAH.

**[[prop:prop_ebot_addendum_1040|ADDENDUM — 1040 BF, on release.]]** The demand above was filed and is still, at the date of this release, unanswered. The company that could have answered it no longer exists. Waluigi has therefore done the only remaining useful thing and published the day itself: the bridge is armed, the sentry does not speak, the slope returns its dead, and four humans are named on a plank past the span with the fourth name rubbed nearly out. None of that has aged. A mountain does not care which year you reach it in. WAH.
